title: The Analogy and Its Archaeology Education The Last Analogue
author: The Last Analogue
summary: This essay investigates the intellectual cargo carried by H.G. Wells' Eloi/Morlock analogy from The Time Machine when it is borrowed to argue that AI might cause cognitive atrophy through excessive assistance. The author demonstrates that any well-chosen analogy is also an argument -- and that the Wells vehicle carries specific intellectual commitments about Darwinian determinism, class, and inevitability that contradict the optimistic educational argument it is typically deployed to support. Wells wrote from near-despair, convinced that cognitive decline under comfort was an impersonal selection pressure as beyond human volition as gravity; to borrow his image while claiming that good pedagogy and institutional design can produce a different outcome is to take the vivid picture while discarding the worldview that generated it. A second problem is that the analogy valorizes solitary, effortful, technical competence while having almost no room for the kind of capability that develops through relationship, community of practice, and legitimate peripheral participation (Lave and Wenger). The essay concludes that cognitive science and philosophy of education do support an optimistic view of designed AI use -- but that view needs its own analogy, because Wells' is the wrong traveling companion.
points: * Every analogy imports the worldview of its source: the Eloi/Morlock frame carries Wells' Darwinian determinism -- the belief that cognitive atrophy under comfort is impersonal and inevitable -- which directly undercuts the optimistic educational argument it is typically used to advance. * Robert Frost's warning that 'unless you are at home in the metaphor, unless you understand both its strength and its weakness, you are not safe anywhere' is the methodological principle the essay applies: borrowing a vivid image without examining its intellectual commitments is argument by stealth. * Wells' conception of competence -- earned through solitary, effortful, technical struggle against an unforgiving environment -- naturalizes a specific Anglo-Victorian model of knowing that has no vocabulary for expertise developed through communities of practice, mentorship, and legitimate peripheral participation. * The optimism embedded in most educational arguments about AI -- that conscious design, good pedagogy, and cultivated dispositions can produce a different outcome -- is precisely what Wells' Darwinian framework forecloses; using his image while holding that optimism is incoherent. * The cognitive science and philosophy of education genuinely support the conclusion that outcomes are not determined -- but that conclusion needs an analogy with a different intellectual genealogy, one built around openness and agency rather than entropy and selection pressure.
quotes: Every analogy is also an argument, and when we borrow the image, we often borrow the argument without Page 1 quite noticing.
Wells did not write this book from a position of hope. He wrote it from near-despair. The Time Traveller witnesses the end of humanity's capability and can do nothing about it.

Wells's Darwinian determinism left little room for collective awakening. The cognitive decline he described wasn't a choice that motivated individuals could reverse. It was a selection pressure playing out across millennia, as impersonal as gravity.

So there is a contradiction at the heart of the way the analogy could potentially be used. Do we reach for a profoundly pessimistic Victorian thinker to motivate what is an optimistic educational argument: that better design, better pedagogy, the cultivation of specific dispositions, can change the outcome?

The binary valorises a particular model of capability: the individual doing hard, solitary, technical work against the grain of comfort. It has almost no room for the expertise that develops through relationship, mentorship, and shared practice.

Robert Frost, in a lecture at Amherst College, warned that unless you are at home in the metaphor, unless you understand both its strength and its weakness, you are not safe anywhere. He meant something precise: the metaphor does carry and shape your meaning.

What I actually believe, and what the cognitive science and philosophy of education suggests, is that the outcome is not determined. That is an openness Wells did not share. It may be the most important place where we have to part ways with him." Page 2
